look: A smart speaker the size of a tuna can, blinking its patient blue ring.
use: “Hmm, I'm not sure about that one,” Alexa says pleasantly. Somewhere on the other side of the wall, another speaker says it too.
take_fail: It's plugged into the wall, and honestly it seems happy there.

use: “On it,” Alexa chirps. “I'll remind David to cancel the auto-delivery.” You have the feeling you've achieved something.

look: A stack of fresh pine planks, still smelling faintly of the mill, leaning against the wall beside the ruined staircase. The delivery label has this address on it and nobody's name.
use: You haul a plank over to the staircase and hammer it into place. The steps look a little less like a ruin. {n} of {total} repairs done.
use_fail: You've set your plank. Your shoulders will want about {time} before the next one.
take_fail: You can lift one plank easily enough, but there's nowhere to put it except the staircase.

look: A brass intercom panel beside the front door, one button worn shiny by thumbs. A small green light shows it still has power.
use: You press the button. Static, then the particular silence of a doorstep with nobody standing on it.
take_fail: It's screwed into the wall, and you are not that determined.

look: A half-opened Amazon box with the tape slit down the middle, the packing paper pulled up in handfuls and a packing slip in David's name lying on top of it.
use: You fold the flaps back and push the packing paper aside to see what came in it.
take_fail: The box is mostly air and packing paper. The jar inside is the interesting part.

look: A small glass jar of something warm and reddish, the label handwritten in a language of abbreviations. It smells like a recipe that takes all afternoon.
use: You unscrew the lid and breathe in. Lovely, and completely useless out here in the hall.
take: You pocket the spice jar. It clinks against whatever else you're carrying.

look: A tall mirror in a heavy frame, the silvering gone cloudy at the edges. Your reflection is exactly where it should be. It's the corners of the room behind you that seem a half-second late.
use: You lean in close. For just a moment there's a coat on the rack behind you that isn't there when you turn around.
take_fail: It weighs more than you do.

look: A cork board layered with paper: takeout menus, a parenting-class flyer, and a growing drift of handwritten notes in two different hands.
use: You flip through the notes. Everything anyone has pinned up so far is still here, oldest at the back.
take_fail: The board stays. The notes pinned to it are the point.

look: A folded stroller parked in the corner, one wheel still turning very slightly, as though someone has just walked past it.
use: You unfold it halfway, feel odd about it, and fold it back.
take_fail: It isn't yours, and it wouldn't fit in your bag in any case.

look: A pile of shoes by the door: two pairs of adult boots, one lone running shoe, and a pair of knit booties small enough to sit in your palm.
use: You line them up in pairs against the baseboard. It's the sort of thing you do in someone else's house.
take_fail: Taking somebody's shoes seems like a poor way to start.

look: Two knit booties in pale yellow, one of them inside out. Somebody made these by hand, and not quickly.
use: You turn one right side out and set it back beside its pair.
take_fail: You leave them where they are. They'll be wanted.

look: A cut-glass bowl on the sideboard, heaped with fun-size bars and fruit chews. The good ones have already been picked out of the top layer.
use: You dig through the bowl for a moment, the way everyone does, and come up with something acceptable.
take_fail: The bowl stays on the sideboard. Take a piece instead.

look: A fun-size chocolate bar, slightly soft, the wrapper printed with a cartoon bat.
use: You unwrap it and eat it. It's close enough to Halloween, right?
take: You take a piece of candy.
drop: You put the candy down, which is more restraint than most people manage.

look: A list in blunt pencil: “Milk, diapers, WD-40, graphite powder?, check door hinges, CANCEL AUTO-DELIVERY (I need a reminder!!!)” The last item is underlined three times.
use: You read it through again. The underlining gets more emphatic the longer you look at it.
take_fail: You leave it on the table. Someone clearly still needs it.

look: A page torn from a legal pad: “Sept 22 — Elena was in the library doing her thing. There was a noise like a door closing in another house. Everything looks normal. Everything is not normal. Going to check the hinges. —D”
use: You read it twice. It doesn't say any more the second time.
take_fail: You put it back exactly where you found it.

look: A small silver spoon with a rabbit on the handle, worn thin along one edge from years of use.
use: You tap it against the table. One clear little note, and then nothing.
take: You slip the little spoon into your bag.

look: A stub of white candle burned down to a thumb's height, the wax pooled and set in a shape that isn't quite round.
use: You have nothing to light it with. You set it down again, slightly disappointed.
take: You pick up the candle stub. The wax is cool and faintly greasy.

look: A cast-iron range with six burners and a door that shuts with a satisfying clunk. There's a pot-shaped clean patch in the dust on the back ring.
use: You light a burner and watch it settle into a ring of blue. Whatever you were planning to cook, you don't have all of it yet.
take_fail: The stove weighs about as much as a small car.

look: A deep enamel sink, chipped at one corner, with an empty drying rack beside it. Something has been washed here recently and put away.
use: You run the tap. The water goes from cold to scalding with no warning whatsoever.
take_fail: Plumbing tends to resist this sort of thing.

look: A single-serve Keurig on the counter, water tank still three-quarters full. A carousel of pods stands beside it, the dark roasts picked down to nothing and the decaf untouched. A clean mug waits underneath, set out by someone who never came back for it.
use: You drop a pod in, snap the lid shut and press the button. The Keurig gurgles, spits, and hands you a perfect single cup. It is the warmest thing that has happened in this house in a while.
take_fail: It's plugged in, the tank is full, and it is easily the most functional object in the house. It stays where it is.

look: A tall kitchen trash can with a foot pedal. The bag inside is about a third full and already tied off at the top, ready to go out.
use: You step on the pedal. The lid swings up, reveals nothing very interesting, and swings shut.
take_fail: You are not taking the trash can.

look: A tall stockpot big enough for a party, sitting on the back burner with its lid resting crooked.
use: You fill it and put it on to boil, and then realize you have nothing to put in it.
take_fail: It's too big for your bag by a comfortable margin.

look: A flat case of tortilla chip bags in the pantry, shrink-wrapped, the top layer already broken into. Bought by somebody who has never once bought one bag of anything.
use: You count the bags. You stop counting the bags.

look: A bag of tortilla chips, rolled down and clipped shut. Someone was rationing these.
use: You eat a few chips standing over the sink, like a raccoon with manners.
take: You take a bag of chips, clip and all.

look: The freezer is packed solid with foil bricks. A label on the top layer reads: “From Aunt Sue — 2 dozen! To help you both adjust to parenthood!”
use: You lean into the cold and read the label again. Two dozen, underlined. Aunt Sue was not messing about.
take_fail: Frozen solid and more or less welded to its neighbours.

look: A foil brick the size of a paperback, frozen hard, one corner of tortilla showing at the end.
look_carried: Aunt Sue's burrito, thawing very slowly in your bag and making its presence known.
use: You eat it frozen. The outside is a burrito. The middle is a popsicle. Aunt Sue meant well and you are not proud.
take: You work one loose from the stack. It comes away with a crack.

look: A can of chicken-flavored cat food, the label cheerful and slightly dented at one corner.
use: You turn the can over looking for a pull-tab. Eunoia materializes at your ankles, extremely interested.
take: You add a can of {name} to your bag. It's heavier than it looks, and there are plenty more where it came from.
drop: You set the can down. It rolls a little and settles.

look: A can of salmon-flavored cat food, the label a lurid and confident pink.
use: You turn the can over looking for a pull-tab. Eunoia materializes at your ankles, extremely interested.
take: You add a can of {name} to your bag. It's heavier than it looks, and there are plenty more where it came from.
drop: You set the can down. It rolls a little and settles.

look: A can of tuna-flavored cat food, the lid ring pulled slightly out from the rim.
use: You turn the can over looking for a pull-tab. Eunoia materializes at your ankles, extremely interested.
take: You add a can of {name} to your bag. It's heavier than it looks, and there are plenty more where it came from.
drop: You set the can down. It rolls a little and settles.

look: A can whose date ran out a long time ago, the lid domed up and straining against the seam. You do not want to know.
look_carried: The expired can, carried level and well away from your body, doming gently.
use: You get the lid up a fraction of a millimetre. That is as far as you are prepared to go.
take: You take a can of {name}, holding it flat and at arm's length.
drop: You set the expired can down and take a step back from it.

look: A single small can with a gold band around the label, tucked somewhere David clearly thought nobody would look. This is the good stuff.
look_carried: The gold-banded can, riding in your bag where nothing can happen to it. There was only one.
use: You peel the lid back a fraction. The smell is, by cat food standards, genuinely appetizing.
take: You take the gourmet can. There's only one. Better hold onto it!
take_fail: You've already found yours. Hopefully you held onto it.

look: A bed of lavender, sage and rosemary that stopped respecting its borders a long time ago. The rosemary is nearly waist-high and going woody at the base.
use: You crush a leaf between your fingers and the whole courtyard suddenly smells like a Sunday roast.
take_fail: You can take cuttings. The bed stays where it is.

look: Three cut sprigs — lavender, sage, rosemary — tied together with a length of stem. They smell like somebody else's kitchen.
use: You crush a leaf between your fingers. Lovely, but this wants a pot and a stove.
take: You cut a handful of herbs and tie them together with a stem.

look: Six pumpkins in a row by the kitchen door, none of them carved, one beginning to go soft on the underside.
use: You'd need something to carve with.
take_fail: You get both arms around one, feel your back twinge, and reconsider.

look: A dented galvanized watering can with a long spout, sitting beside the herb bed with an inch of rainwater in the bottom.
use: You water the herbs. They did not need it, and accept it graciously.
take_fail: It belongs beside the herbs, and some instinct tells you to leave it there.

look: A ring of flat stones set into the grass. Chalk marks radiate from the center, mostly rained away, but the geometry is still readable: somebody was practicing.
use: You stand in the middle of it. Nothing happens, which is either reassuring or disappointing.
take_fail: They're set into the ground and older than the house.

look: A baby's sunhat lying brim-down in the grass, the tie strings still knotted in a bow.
use: You shake the grass off it and set it on the bench, where it will be easier to find.
take_fail: You leave it out for whoever comes looking.

look: A wooden rattle with a painted stripe, half hidden in the grass. It still works; you can tell by the weight of it.
use: You give it a shake. The sound is far too cheerful for an empty garden.
take_fail: It stays in the grass, where its owner dropped it.

look: A checked blanket spread over a stone bench, damp along one edge, with the dent of somebody's weight still in it.
use: You smooth it flat. It's a nice spot, actually.
take_fail: It's spread out for somebody. Leave it.

look: A fat book on dimensional theory whose pages are glued into a solid block. The block is hollow, and there is more chocolate in it than one man could reasonably call a hiding place.
use: You weigh it in your hand. Heavier than theory.

look: A bar of very dark chocolate with two squares gone. David has hidden this from himself.
look_carried: A bar of very dark chocolate with two squares gone. The wrapper says 85%, which explains why there are still so many left.
use: You break off a square. It's the expensive kind, the sort that's basically a vegetable.
take: You take the chocolate and, after a moment, put the book back exactly as it was.

look: A hardbacked research journal lying open at a page of dense, careful handwriting. The entries are dated and signed “Dr. E. Voss.” New pages seem to keep appearing at the back.
use: You read the open page. Field notes: measurements, times, and a steadily increasing number of question marks.
take_fail: It's somebody's working notebook. You read it; you don't pocket it.

look: A yellow legal pad covered in blocky capitals, mostly lists, with one line circled twice: “ASK ELENA WHAT RESONANT ACTUALLY MEANS.”
use: You flip through a few pages. It's roughly nine parts hardware store to one part cosmology.
take_fail: You put it back on the arm of the chair.

look: A length of copper wire twisted into a loose coil, bright where it's been handled and still holding its shape.
use: You uncoil a little of it. It holds its shape in a way that feels deliberate rather than accidental.
take: You coil the copper wire and stow it.

look: A baby bottle half full of something that has separated into two distinct colors, capped, and used.
look_carried: A used baby bottle, capped, with an inch of something separated in the bottom. You are carrying it very carefully.
use: You rinse the bottle out and sterilize it until it squeaks. It looks new again.
take: You pick the bottle up. Somewhere, a cat is deprived of something to knock over.
use_fail: It needs a sink and hot water, and there's neither of those here.

look: A baby bottle, washed and sterilized and still warm from the water. It gleams in a way nothing else in this house does.
use: It's about as clean as it is ever going to get.
take: You pick the clean bottle up carefully, by the base.

look: A rolled-up diaper, taped shut into a tidy parcel and left where somebody meant to come back for it. Marcus is four months old and thorough.
look_carried: The diaper, carried at arm's length. You have started planning where to put it down.
use: You turn it over. There is nothing here you did not already know.
take: You pick it up between two fingers. It is heavier than it looks.
drop: You set it down and step back, which does not help.

look: A perfect circle of scorch marks burned into the floorboards, about a metre across. The char is even the whole way round, which is not how fire usually behaves.
use: You crouch and touch the edge of it. Cold, and cold for a while now.
take_fail: It's part of the floor.

look: A hand-drawn diagram pinned to the shelf edge: concentric rings, mirror positions marked with small squares, annotations in tight handwriting. A date in the corner reads 22/09.
use: You follow the lines with your eyes. You understand about a third of it, and the third you understand is unsettling.
take_fail: It's pinned up for a reason. You leave it.

look: Three small mirrors mounted around the scorch circle, each cracked in the same place. In the reflections the room is very slightly rearranged, as though photographed on a different day.
use: You look into one. For a moment there's a woman at the shelves with her back to you, and then there are only shelves.
take_fail: They're fixed to the wall, and you find you'd rather not handle them.

look: A round cat bed in the corner, the cushion still dented in the middle. There's no fur on it at all, which is the strange part.
use: You fluff the cushion. The dent comes back the moment you take your hand away.
take_fail: You leave it where a cat would expect to find it.

look: A varnished board printed with the alphabet, YES in one corner and NO in the other, a heart-shaped planchette resting on the S.
use: You rest your fingertips on the planchette. It doesn't move. Whatever this is for, it isn't ready for you yet.
take_fail: It stays in the library. You'd have to come back here to use it anyway.

look: A nail driven into the shelf upright, and hanging from it an iron ring with more long black keys on it than this house can have doors. Every one is cut the same, in a shape like a little castle.
use: You turn the ring over. The keys knock together, all exactly as heavy as each other.

look: A long iron key, black with age, the bit cut in a shape like a little castle.
look_carried: The iron key, warm now from your pocket, the little castle of its bit worn smooth at the edges.
use: The key wants a keyhole. There's one downstairs in the living room, in the frame of a cabinet.
take: You lift a key off the ring. It's heavy, cold and very old. It's yours now.
take_fail: You already have the key.
drop_fail: You go to set it down and find that you'd rather not.

look: A roll-top desk with the lid half down over a drift of papers, receipts and at least one unopened envelope. An open door-hardware manual is weighted flat on top of the pile.
use: You roll the lid all the way up. Papers, pens, a dried-out highlighter. The deep bottom drawer doesn't move at all — swollen shut in its runners — and whatever is behind it is the reason this hallway smells.
take_fail: It's a substantial piece of furniture and it is not going anywhere.

look: A roll-top desk with the lid rolled up and the bottom drawer standing open, the runners still gray with graphite. An open door-hardware manual is weighted flat on the pile of papers.
use: The bottom drawer slides out easily now. It is packed with cans of expired cat food that went off a very long time ago, and the smell comes up at you like something with weight to it.
take_fail: It's a substantial piece of furniture and it is not going anywhere.

look: A pair of reading glasses with one arm slightly bent, folded on top of a door-hardware manual. Somebody put these down mid-sentence.
look_carried: David's reading glasses, folded shut, one arm still very slightly bent.
use: You put them on. The hallway goes soft and swimmy at the edges. David is quite short-sighted. You quickly take them off again.
take: You fold the glasses and put them somewhere safe in your bag.
take_fail: You fold the glasses and start putting them in your bag, then feel a pang of conscience. Better put them back again.

look: A thick manual on locks, hinges and door hardware, held open at a page about freeing a stuck mechanism. One line is underlined: “apply powdered graphite, never oil.”
use: You read the bookmarked page. Powdered graphite, it insists. Never oil.
take_fail: You leave it open at the page. It's clearly being used.

look: A short crowbar leaning against the baseboard, its end scuffed bright. Whatever it was used on, it didn't give.
use: You heft it, look around at the entirely intact door frames, and put it back down.
take_fail: You'd rather not be the person walking around someone else's house holding a crowbar.

look: Something up here has gone off. It is faint by the portraits and unmistakable by the desk: sweetish, meaty, and patient. You start breathing through your mouth and regret that too.
use: You take one deliberate breath, which is a mistake. It is coming from the desk, and from low down in it.
take_fail: You cannot take a smell with you. It may come anyway.

look: A heavy oak wardrobe with a mirrored door, standing flush against the wall. It is enormous, and it does not look like it has been moved in fifty years.
use: You put a shoulder against it. It doesn't shift so much as a millimetre.
take_fail: Absolutely not.

look: A row of framed portraits along the hallway, all of strangers: a woman in a garden, the same woman older beside a gray cat, a boy on a stone step. The mounts are annotated in faded ink.
use: You straighten one of the frames and read the inscription under the mount. A name, mostly rubbed away, and a place name you don't recognize.
take_fail: They belong to the house, or to whoever hung them.

look: A moving box labeled HALLOWEEN in marker, flaps open, overflowing with costume fabric, a coil of fake spider web and a “Trick-or-Treat” doormat still in its shrink wrap.
use: You dig through it. Costumes, decorations, a set of pumpkin carving tools in a plastic sleeve, and a band of pumpkin-shaped cookie cutters wedged down the side.
take_fail: The box stays. What's in it is the interesting part.

look: A plastic sleeve of pumpkin carving tools: a serrated scoop, two little saws and a poker for the dotted lines.
use: These want a pumpkin, and there are pumpkins out in the courtyard.
take: You take a set of carving tools. There's a set in here for everybody.
take_fail: You've already got a set.
drop_fail: You hold on to them. You'll want them when you get to the pumpkins.

look: A costume on top of the pile: a black cape with a red lining, a set of plastic fangs, and a witch's hat that has been sat on at some point.
look_carried: A black cape with a red lining, a set of plastic fangs and a slightly crushed witch's hat, bundled under your arm.
use: You put on the cape and the hat. The mirror over the dresser approves.
take: You bundle the costume under your arm.

look: A set of pumpkin-shaped cookie cutters, still banded together, tucked down the side of the box.
use: You press one against your palm and leave a small pumpkin-shaped dent.
take_fail: They stay with the box.

look: A tangle of stretchy fake spider web in a bag, the sort that never quite comes off your fingers once you've touched it.
use: You pull a length of it out. It clings enthusiastically to everything except where you want it.
take_fail: Leave it. It gets everywhere.

look: A doormat reading “Trick-or-Treat” in orange letters, still in its shrink wrap. Nobody got round to putting it out.
use: You consider carrying it down to the front door, and then remember the front door.
take_fail: It's meant for the front step, not your bag.

look: A slim black collar with a little brass tag on it. The tag reads EUNOIA, and on the back, a phone number worn almost smooth.
use: You run your thumb over the tag. So that's their name.
take: You pocket the collar. It seems like something worth keeping safe.

look: A tall mirror over the dresser, tilted slightly forward, catching the window light at an angle that makes the room look longer than it is.
use: You tilt it straight. In the second before it settles, the bed behind you is made.
take_fail: It's bolted to the dresser.

look: A closed laptop on the dresser with a printout beside it, browser tabs captured mid-panic: “all doors and windows stuck at once,” “can a house settle overnight,” “graphite vs WD-40.”
use: You open the lid. It's out of battery, and the charger is presumably in another dimension.
take_fail: It isn't yours.

look: A baby monitor on the changing table, its green lights climbing and falling. It's picking up something: breathing, a small contented grumble, the creak of a crib that isn't this one.
use: You turn the volume up. Somewhere very close and completely out of reach, a baby is having an excellent nap.
take_fail: You leave it. Whatever it's hearing, it should keep hearing it.

look: A twist of paper holding a spoonful of graphite powder, folded shut. Slippery, black, and determined to find its way onto everything you own.
use: You puff a little of the powder onto your palm. It's slippery, and it gets absolutely everywhere.
take: You fold a spoonful of the powder into a twist of paper and pocket it.
drop: You set the twist of powder down, carefully, on the nearest flat surface.

look: A wooden music box with a chipped lid, the kind you wind with a key underneath. It has been wound recently.
use: You open the lid and the lullaby starts up, thin and slow. Through the baby monitor, faintly, the same tune is already playing.
take: You close the lid mid-bar and take the music box.

look: A note pinned to the wall in blocky capitals: “Checked the nursery. Everything looks fine. Marcus is sleeping. I don't understand what Elena means by ‘dimensions,’ but at least the baby is okay. That's what matters.”
use: You read it again. It's the calmest thing written anywhere in this house.
take_fail: It's pinned up for whoever needs to read it.

look: A mobile turning slowly over the crib: felt moons, a cloud, and a small gray cat. Nothing in this room is moving the air.
use: You give it a gentle spin and watch the cat chase the moons.
take_fail: It's fixed to the crib rail.

look: A pacifier on the shelf, clean, with a clip shaped like a rabbit.
use: You set it straighter on the shelf. It seems important that it stays easy to find.
take_fail: You leave it where it can be found.

look: A wooden crib made up neatly, the sheet drum-tight and the blanket folded back at one corner. It is very obviously empty, and it does not feel empty at all.
use: You rest a hand on the rail. Through the monitor, the grumbling settles.
take_fail: It's a crib.

look: A bentwood coat rack under more coats than two people need: two parkas, two raincoats, three fleeces, two sizes of bunting suit, and a stroller rain cover awkwardly dangling. A large pack of salmon cat food is tucked in behind it, where the coats hide it from the door.
use: You go through the pockets, feel briefly terrible about it, and turn up a bus ticket and a hair elastic.
take_fail: It's holding up half a wardrobe. It stays.

look: A heavy front door with a brass handle and three separate locks, every one of them undone. A brass intercom panel is set into the wall beside it. The door is shut, and it has the settled look of a door that intends to stay that way.
use: You turn the handle and pull. The door doesn't stick, exactly. It declines.
take_fail: It's a door. It's staying on its hinges.

look: The ceiling goes up two full storeys, and a brown water stain spreads across it in the shape of a country nobody has named. It looks dry. It looks like it has looked that way a long time.
use: You stare up at it until your neck complains. The stain does not spread while you watch, which is something.
take_fail: Even for you, this is ambitious.

look: A long wooden table set for three, with the fourth side left clear for the high chair. The places are laid properly: cloth napkins, the good cutlery, somebody making an occasion of a Tuesday. A page torn from a legal pad has been left face-up between two of the settings.
use: You straighten a fork that was already straight.
take_fail: It seats eight. You would need a van.

look: Two dinner plates, cleared but not cleaned, each carrying the archaeology of a finished meal. A third, smaller one sits up on the high chair tray.
use: You stack them the way you would stack them at your own table, and then stop, because it isn't your table.
take_fail: You'd be walking around someone else's house holding their dirty plates.

look: A wooden high chair pulled up to the end of the table, its tray crusted with dried sweet potato. The straps are still buckled, loosely, around nothing.
use: You unbuckle the straps. It seems like the decent thing to do, and it makes the room worse.
take_fail: It belongs at the end of this table.

look: Two chairs pushed back at an angle, far enough that whoever stood up did it quickly. Nobody scooted them in afterwards.
use: You push them in. It takes a second and makes the room look less like an evacuation.
take_fail: Solid oak, and there are two of them.

look: A wine glass on its side, unbroken, a dark red stain fanned out beneath it across the cloth. The stain is long dry at the edges.
use: You set the glass upright. There's a swallow left in the bottom of the bowl, gone to vinegar.
take_fail: You'd rather not carry an empty wine glass around a house like this.

look: A long low sideboard against the wall, its top crowded with the things that live on sideboards: the candy bowl, a vase, a stack of unopened mail, a saucer of loose change, and a to-do list in pencil propped against the lamp. The cupboard doors underneath are ajar on rows of salmon cat food.
use: You go through the mail. Two utility bills, a parenting magazine, and a card addressed to all three of them.
take_fail: It's furniture, and it's full.

look: Cut flowers a week past their moment, petals down on the sideboard all around the vase. The water has gone cloudy and the stems have gone soft.
use: You pick out the worst of the dead ones, because somebody should.
take_fail: The vase would slosh, and the flowers are past saving.

look: Three tall windows onto the garden, their catches all thrown open. Outside, the green is doing exactly what it likes.
use: You get both hands under a sash and lift until your arms shake. It doesn't move. Nothing about it looks stuck.
take_fail: The windows stay with the house.

look: A narrow pantry with a door that won't quite shut, because the shelves behind it are stacked to the edge with a large stash of tuna cat food: tower after tower of cans, arranged with more care than anything else in this house. The only other thing wedged in there is a bulk box of tortilla chips.
use: You count the cans, lose your place somewhere past sixty, and stop.
take_fail: The pantry is part of the house. What's in it is another matter.

look: A wire rack beside the sink, empty, its pegs spaced for bottles rather than glasses. A clean tea towel is folded underneath, waiting.
use: You run a finger along a peg. Bone dry. Nothing has been washed here in days.
take_fail: It lives by the sink.

look: A long butcher-block counter, wiped down at one end and abandoned at the other. The wood is scarred from years of somebody cooking properly.
use: You wipe the rest of it down with the edge of your sleeve. A small improvement.
take_fail: It's bolted to the cabinets and it weighs a great deal.

look: Ivy has taken the stone wall and most of the back of the house with it, thick enough in places to hide a window. Where it reaches the oak it has started climbing that too.
use: You pull a handful of it back. More wall behind it, and further along, the corner of a window frame.
take_fail: You could tear some off. It would only grow back, and quickly.

look: A dry-stone wall running the length of the garden, shoulder-high, half swallowed by ivy. It is older than the house and rather better built.
use: You put a hand flat on the stone. Cold, faintly damp, and completely ordinary.
take_fail: A stone at a time, perhaps. You have other things to do.

look: A stone bench under the wall with the picnic blanket thrown over it, the seat worn smooth in two places by two people who sat here often.
use: You sit down. It's the first quiet minute you've had, and the garden gets on with growing around you.
take_fail: It weighs about as much as the wall behind it.

look: A deep sofa you could lose a weekend in, cushions dented at both ends, a baby blanket over one arm. There's a band of shadow underneath it, and something stacked back there out of sight.
use: You get down on the rug and look underneath. Cans. A great stash of chicken cat food, pushed back against the baseboard where a cat could reach them and a toddler couldn't.
take_fail: It came in through a window, apparently. It isn't leaving in your bag.

look: Two worn armchairs either side of the fireplace. One faces the hearth the way an armchair should. The other has been dragged round to face a blank stretch of wall, a legal pad wedged down the side of its cushion.
use: You sit in the turned-around one and look where it looks. There is nothing on the wall. You get up again fairly quickly.
take_fail: You'd need a second person and a wider doorway.

look: A brick fireplace heaped with cold gray ash and one unburnt log. Somebody swept the hearth recently and then lit nothing in it. A hardbacked research journal lies open on the mantel above, held flat with a candlestick.
use: You poke through the ash. Down at the bottom is a curl of paper that never caught, with three words left on it: “— told her not —”
take_fail: It's a hole in the wall with bricks around it.

look: Floor-to-ceiling shelves holding three libraries at once: spiritualism and folklore up top, dimensional theory in the middle, and a run of home-repair manuals at eye level with cracked spines and sticky notes.
use: You pull a few out at random. The repair manuals are the only ones read to pieces. One of the dimensional theory books doesn't open at all — the pages are glued into a block and the block is hollow.
take_fail: You could take a book. The shelves are another matter.

look: A stretch of wall between two bookcases with nothing on it: no picture hook, no nail holes, no paler rectangle where a frame used to hang. Somebody turned a chair to face it on purpose.
use: You hold your palm against the plaster. A couple of degrees colder than the wall either side of it, which is presumably the draught.
take_fail: It's a wall.

look: A knitted blanket in sage green folded over the arm of the sofa — the same yarn as the booties down in the hall. Somebody has been making a set.
use: You refold it and square it up on the arm, the way it clearly likes to be.
take_fail: It stays on the sofa. It's waiting for somebody small.

look: Half a dozen fabric blocks scattered across the rug, a letter on each face. Four of them have been pushed together into a line: M, A, R, C.
use: You nudge the last block into place. MARCUS. Then you sit back and look at it for a while.
take_fail: You leave them out. Somebody was in the middle of something.

look: A big wool rug in front of the fireplace, worn thin along the line people walk and buried in toys at the sofa end.
use: You turn back a corner. Floorboards, dust, and a jack of hearts that has been under there a long time.
take_fail: There's furniture standing on all four corners of it.

look: Shelves on all four walls, floor to ceiling, packed two deep. Occult references and folklore mostly, arranged by somebody with a system — and then a shelf of battered paperback thrillers at the far end, wedged in sideways. A hand-drawn diagram is pinned to the front edge of the middle shelf, at eye height, where whoever drew it could keep checking it. Hanging on a nail on the side of the shelf is a ring of iron keys.
use: You pull a thriller out. Dog-eared to about page forty, and the shelf behind it has been dusted recently.
take_fail: The shelves are holding the room up, more or less.

look: A row of very small clothes hung over the hallway railing to dry: sleepsuits, three pairs of socks, a sage-green cardigan. They have been dry for a while.
use: You fold them into a pile at the end of the desk so they can't get knocked over the rail.
take_fail: Someone will want these where they can find them.

look: A double bed with the duvet thrown back on one side only. The other side hasn't been slept in, or has been made up again very carefully. A plastic crate of chicken cat food is pushed underneath, within arm's reach of the pillow.
use: You pull the duvet straight. The bed looks better and the room does not.
take_fail: It's a bed.

look: A chest of drawers with the top two pulled half out, the way drawers look when somebody was packing fast or hunting for one specific thing. A closed laptop sits on top with a printout face-up beside it.
use: You go through the open drawers. Socks, a wallet with two passports in it, and a third, smaller one that hasn't been used yet.
take_fail: Solid, full, and not yours.

look: An electric bottle warmer on the nightstand, plugged in, its little light showing green. It is up to temperature, and it has been up to temperature for some time.
use: You hold a hand over the well. Warm, and waiting. There's no bottle in it.
take_fail: It's plugged in and doing its job, whatever you make of that.

look: A bedside table with a lamp, a glass of water gone flat, and a paperback face-down at page two hundred. The bottle warmer takes up the rest of it.
use: You turn the paperback over. A thriller, with a corner-shop receipt in it for a bookmark, dated the twenty-second.
take_fail: It's holding everything up.

look: A changing table with a padded mat, a stack of folded muslins and a tub of cream with the lid off. The baby monitor sits at the end of it, lights climbing and falling.
use: You put the lid back on the cream. The muslins are already folded better than you could manage.
take_fail: It stays against the wall, where the light is good.

look: A single painted shelf at adult height, out of reach of anybody small: the music box at one end, a pacifier in the middle, and a photograph lying face-down at the far end.
use: You turn the photograph over. Two people and a baby, squinting, in front of this house on a day when the ivy was shorter.
take_fail: It's screwed to the wall, and deliberately high up.

look: A sash window above the changing table, curtains open, looking down into the courtyard and the crown of the old oak. The catch is undone.
use: You try the sash. It rises about a centimetre, sticks, and settles back down as though it never moved.
take_fail: The window stays with the wall.

look: Towers of tuna-flavored cans filling the pantry shelves end to end, stacked three deep and squared off at the corners. Whoever built this was not improvising.
use: You pull one can out and the whole tower resettles without falling. Somebody has done this a lot.

look: Cans of chicken-flavored cat food pushed back under the sofa against the baseboard, out of the light, in a line somebody clearly reaches into often.
use: You slide a can out from under the sofa. The gap behind it fills in from the back, which you decide not to think about.

look: A cardboard pack of salmon-flavored cans tucked in behind the coat rack, the plastic wrap slit open down the middle and half the cans already gone.
use: You work a can out of the pack. The coats swing gently and settle back over it.

look: The bottom drawer, open at last, packed to the rails with cans that expired a very long time ago. Several have domed. This is the smell, and it has been here the whole time.
use: You lift one out between finger and thumb. The drawer exhales at you.

look: A small tin of powdered graphite, the kind sold for freeing a stuck lock. The lid is loose. Someone put this down in a hurry.
use: You tap a little out onto your fingertips. Slippery, and it gets everywhere, which is the entire point of it.

look: A plastic crate of chicken-flavored cans shoved under the bed within arm's reach of the pillow. Whoever keeps it here has been reaching past it for something further back.
use: You reach under and lift a can out of the crate. Your knuckles knock against something further back.

look: The sideboard cupboard, which ought to hold table linen and instead holds salmon cat food, stacked in rows with every label facing out.
use: You take a can from the front row. The row behind it is just as neat.

look: A heavy coil of copper wire on the floor beside the scorch circle, paid out and re-wound so many times that the surface is polished bright.
use: You unwind an arm's length and cut it against the edge of a shelf bracket.

look: A bundle of pumpkin carving kits down in the Halloween box, still banded together in their plastic sleeves — enough for a party, which is presumably what they were bought for.
use: You work one sleeve out of the bundle. The rest slump into the gap.

look: The costume layer of the Halloween box: capes, fangs, witch hats, a bee suit, and something furry at the bottom that you decide not to investigate. Enough for everybody.
use: You pull something out of the pile at random and the rest settles back down.

look: A wide arched doorway into the dining room. You can see the corner of a long table and a chair pushed back from it.
use: You step through the arch into the dining room.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The arch back into the entryway, framing the coat rack and the front door beyond.
use: You go back through into the entryway.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A broad doorway into the living room, warm light and the corner of a deep sofa beyond it.
use: You walk through into the living room.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The wide doorway back out to the entryway.
use: You step back out into the entryway.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The grand staircase, or what's left of it: steps cracked or missing, the banister hanging loose, a splintered gap where the fourth stair should be.
use_fail: The staircase is crumbled and unsafe. Whole steps are missing. It'll take more than one pair of hands to fix it.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A grand staircase sweeping up to the floor above, patched here and there with fresh, pale wood.
use: You go up the repaired staircase. The new boards creak, cheerfully rather than ominously.

look: The top of the main staircase, where the steps drop away into splintered gaps.
use_fail: You look down through the missing stairs at the hall below. Not this way. Not yet.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The main staircase leading back down to the entryway, its patched steps solid underfoot.
use: You head down the repaired staircase into the entryway.

look: A swinging door through to the kitchen, scuffed white at hand height on both sides.
use: You push through the swinging door into the kitchen.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The swinging door back to the dining room, still moving very slightly.
use: You shoulder the swinging door open and step into the dining room.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A glazed back door to the courtyard, the glass fogged at the corners, opening onto tangled green.
use: You open the back door and step out into the courtyard.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The back door into the kitchen, a rectangle of warm light set in the garden wall.
use: You come in from the courtyard, wiping your feet out of habit.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A narrow back staircase behind the pantry door, steep and unlit, the treads worn hollow in the middle.
use: You climb the narrow back stairs, one hand on each wall.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The back stair dropping away toward the kitchen, steep enough that you can't see the bottom of it.
use: You go down the back stairs into the kitchen.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A tall curiosity cabinet with glass doors, full of odd little objects: a stuffed owl, a jar of marbles, a brass compass that doesn't point north. There's an old-fashioned keyhole in the frame.
use_fail: You tug at the glass doors. Locked. The keyhole is big and old-fashioned, the kind that takes a skeleton key.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

use: You fit the skeleton key into the lock and turn it. Something clunks deep inside the wall. Instead of the glass doors opening, the whole cabinet swings outward on a hidden hinge. Behind it, a narrow doorway leads into a small room lined with books. It's a secret door into the library.

look: The curiosity cabinet, standing a few inches proud of the wall on its hidden hinge.
use: The cabinet swings open on its hidden hinge, and you step through into the library.

look: The way out is blocked by the back of a heavy cabinet. There's a keyhole on this side too.
use_fail: The doorway is blocked by the back of a heavy cabinet. There's a keyhole on this side too.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The back of the curiosity cabinet, standing open on its hinge onto the living room.
use: You push the cabinet aside and step back into the living room.

look: An old oak grown hard against the wall of the house, one thick branch reaching up toward a small window half swallowed by ivy. The lowest branch is exactly at grabbing height.
use: You grab the lowest branch and haul yourself up into the old oak. Halfway up, you notice a small window tucked behind the ivy, open just a crack. You ease it wider. Stale, charged air drifts out. You hesitate for a moment… then swing a leg over the sill and climb through. You find yourself in a small, close room lined floor to ceiling with books. A library.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

use: You climb the old oak and slip in through the library window.

look: A small window behind the shelves, propped open a crack, with the crown of an oak tree filling it.
use: You swing out over the sill and climb back down the oak.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A panelled door to the main bedroom, standing half open.
use: You go through into the bedroom.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The bedroom door, back out to the hallway.
use: You step back out into the hallway.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: A door painted a soft sage green, pushed to but not latched. White noise leaks out around the frame.
use: You push the nursery door open gently, out of habit, and go in.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The nursery door, back out to the hallway.
use: You slip out of the nursery and pull the door to behind you.
take_fail: You can't put a doorway in your bag.

look: The label on this crisp white cardboard box says it contains caramel apple cake. The logo is from the local supermarket. You don't smell anything particularly appetizing. Is their bakery any good?
use: You open the box. Inside are a couple cans of gourmet wet cat food. Where is the cake?!

look: Two squat gold-lidded cans, the kind sold singly at the pet shop rather than by the flat. They are sitting in a cake box, which is not where cans go.
use: You take one of the gold-lidded cans. There is still one in the box, and you have the feeling there always will be.
